# VW Golf - when do these side lamps turn on?

If you own a 2015 VW Golf equipped with Adaptive Front Lighting (AFS) and pointable HID headlights, you might encounter an "Error: Adaptive Front Lighting" warning in your instrument cluster. The system will often report this fault even if the primary headlight beam seems to function correctly, including its characteristic "wiggle" during startup. Based on the diagnostic logic used by these vehicles, this specific error code typically points to a failure in one of the auxiliary side-illumination bulbs located at the corners of the bumper.

These are distinct from your main headlights or fog lights. They serve as dynamic cornering lamps designed to illuminate the curve of the road when you steer sharply. The confusion often arises because, on many units, these lamps may appear entirely dormant under static conditions. You might park the car with the engine running and high beams engaged, turn the steering wheel fully left or right, activate the turn signals, or even flash the hazard lights, yet see absolutely no illumination from these specific fixtures. This lack of visible activity does not necessarily mean they are non-functional; it often means their trigger conditions have not been met.

The technical implementation behind this behavior relies on a specific sequence of events to activate the cornering lamps. Unlike standard running lights that stay on whenever the ignition is in the "On" position, these units require a combination of three simultaneous inputs:
1.  The vehicle must be moving above a certain threshold (typically around 5 mph or 8 km/h).
2.  The headlights must be turned on.
3.  The steering wheel must be turned significantly away from the center position.

If any one of these conditions is missing, the bulbs will remain dark. This explains why you likely observed zero activity while parked in your driveway or stopped at a traffic light; the motion sensor within the AFS module did not detect forward velocity to authorize activation. Similarly, simply turning the wheel while stationary usually triggers a different logic path, often reserved for static cornering lights that might be integrated differently or simply remain off until the car rolls.

It is also important to consider the role of the turn signals in this equation. While these lamps are designed to assist with cornering visibility rather than just signaling direction, some configurations may activate them when a turn signal is engaged *while* driving and steering is applied. However, relying on the turn signal alone while stationary often yields no result, as the primary trigger remains vehicle motion combined with off-center steering.

When an error message appears despite the lights appearing to do nothing, it frequently indicates that one side of the dual-bulb system has failed internally or blown out. In a typical 2015 Golf setup, this cornering function is often split between two separate bulbs (one for the left turn and one for the right). The vehicle's control module monitors both circuits independently. If the left bulb fails, the system logs an error regarding the AFS circuit integrity, even if the right bulb is perfectly healthy but never gets a chance to prove it because you haven't driven the car while turning sharply.

Replacing these bulbs requires careful attention to type. While some might assume they are specialized LEDs or projectors, the cornering lamps in this specific generation of Golf often utilize standard H7 halogen bulbs. Swapping a blown-out bulb for a matching H7 unit typically resolves the fault code immediately, restoring the dynamic lighting capability without needing complex recalibration. Always verify the bulb type before purchasing, as mixing incompatible technologies can sometimes confuse the AFS module or cause premature failure due to heat management differences.
